name: Babur on the rulers of Hindustan in 1526
text: At the date of my conquest of Hindūstān it was governed by five Musalmān rulers (_pādshāh_)[1711] and two Pagans (_kāfir_). These were the respected and independent rulers, but there were also, in the hills and jungles, many rāīs and rājas, held in little esteem (_kīchīk karīm_). ... There are very many rāīs and rājas on all sides and quarters of Hindūstān, some obedient to Islām, some, because of their remoteness or because their places are fastnesses, not subject to Musalmān rule.
author: person:babur
witness: Babur wrote his Turki memoir in India around 1526-30, as a conqueror explaining his prize; he had every reason to stress how divided and weak his enemies were. Still, his count of five sultans, two rajas and countless lesser chiefs matches what the inscriptions and chronicles show.

name: Babur on how Bengal's throne passed
text: There is indeed this peculiarity of the royal office itself that any person who kills the ruler (_pādshāh_) and seats himself on the throne, becomes ruler himself; amīrs, wazīrs, soldiers and peasants submit to him at once, obey him, and recognize him for the rightful ruler his predecessor in office had been.[1720] Bengalis say, "We are faithful to the throne; we loyally obey whoever occupies it."
author: person:babur
witness: Hearsay: Babur never went to Bengal and reports what Bengalis told him, with an outsider's wonder. The habshi (Abyssinian) coups of the 1480s-90s that he goes on to describe are real, so the rule "kill the king and be king" was not pure legend.

name: Al-Biruni on Mahmud of Ghazni's raids
text: Maḥmûd utterly ruined the prosperity of the country, and performed there wonderful exploits, by which the Hindus became like atoms of dust scattered in all directions, and like a tale of old in the mouth of the people. Their scattered remains cherish, of course, the most inveterate aversion towards all Muslims. This is the reason, too, why Hindu sciences have retired far away from those parts of the country conquered by us, and have fled to places which our hand cannot yet reach, to Kashmîr, Benares, and other places.
author: person:al_biruni
work: Alberuni's India, ch. 1, tr. E.C. Sachau (1888)
witness: Al-Biruni wrote about 1030 while in the service of Mahmud's court, so his judgment that his own patron "utterly ruined" the country is striking. He was explaining why Hindu scholars would not share their learning with Muslims; he had a scholar's interest in that reason. Sachau's Victorian English adds its own tone.

name: Jahangir on the plague of 1616
text: in the 10th year after my accession, a great pestilence appeared in some places in Hindustan. The commencement of this calamity was in the parganahs of the Panjab, and by degrees the contagion spread to the city of Lahore. Many of the people, Musulmans and Hindus, died through this. After this it spread to Sirhind and the Du'ab, until it reached Delhi and the surrounding parganahs and villages, and desolated them. At this day it had greatly diminished. It became known from men of great age and from old histories that this disease had never shown itself in this country [514] (before). Physicians and learned men were questioned as to its cause. Some said that it came because there had been drought for two years in succession and little rain fell: others said it was on account of the corruption of the air which occurred through the drought and scarcity. Some attributed it to other causes.
author: person:jahangir
work: Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, tr. A. Rogers, ed. H. Beveridge (1909)
witness: The emperor's own memoir, written as events happened. Jahangir links the epidemic to two years of drought, as his physicians did, an early statement of the drought-hunger-disease chain that colonial famines later repeated. The disease was probably bubonic plague; his claim that it had never struck India before is doubtful.

name: Keene on Aurangzeb, "the Louis Quatorze of the East"
text: Thus does this great ruler furnish another instance of the familiar but everneeded lesson, that countries may be over-governed. Had he been less anxious to stamp his own image and superscription upon the palaces of princes and the temples of priests; upon the moneys of every market, and upon every human heart and conscience; he might have governed with as much success as his free thinking and pleasure-seeking predecessors. But he was the Louis Quatorze of the East; with less of pomp than his European contemporary, but not less of the lust of conquest, of centralization, and of religious conformity.
author: person:h_g_keene
work: The Fall of the Moghul Empire of Hindustan (1887)
witness: A British Indian civil servant writing for a Victorian public in 1876/1887. Keene's moralising about a bigoted emperor shaped the religious explanation later hardened by Jadunath Sarkar; it also flattered the British as tolerant successors. Read it as historiography, not evidence for 1707.

name: Wheeler on Bengal after the diwani
text: The wealth which the old Nawabs had lavished on their pleasures was at least spent within the three provinces; whereas it was now sent to China to buy tea and silk for the East India Company, or was remitted to England as the private fortunes of the Company's servants. Bengal was drained of its silver ... At last the dreadful famine of 1770-71 desolated and depopulated the whole country. Terrible reports reached England that the Company's servants had leagued with the native officials to buy up all the grain and sell it at famine prices.
author: person:james_talboys_wheeler
witness: Wheeler was a Company-era official and imperial historian writing in 1886, broadly sympathetic to British rule, which makes his admission that Bengal was "drained of its silver" notable. He relays the 1770s accusations of grain hoarding by Company servants as reports, not proven fact.

name: Keynes on the Home Charges
text: 2. The Home Charges, that is, the payments which the Government of India must make _in England_, for interest on debt, pensions, payments to the War Office, Government stores (not chargeable to capital), etc., amount to £19,000,000 or £20,000,000 annually.
author: person:john_maynard_keynes
witness: Keynes wrote as a young India Office clerk turned Cambridge economist, with access to official accounts, and treats the charges as a technical remittance problem, not a moral question. His figure is the gross charge; he notes that new borrowing in London reduced what actually had to be remitted.

name: Busbecq on merit among the Ottomans
text: No distinction is attached to birth among the Turks; the deference to be paid to a man is measured by the position he holds in the public service. There is no fighting for precedence; a man’s place is marked out by the duties he discharges. ... with us there is no opening left for merit; birth is the standard for everything; the prestige of birth is the sole key to advancement in the public service.
author: person:ogier_ghiselin_de_busbecq
work: Turkish Letters, letter 1, tr. Forster and Daniell (1881)
witness: The Habsburg ambassador to Suleiman wrote these letters in the 1550s-60s partly to shame Christian nobles into reform. He idealises the devshirme system at its height; the decline thesis later used such praise as the baseline from which the Ottomans "fell".

name: Marco Polo on the caliph and his treasure
text: So he shut the Calif up in the Treasure Tower, and bade that neither meat nor drink should be given him, saying, “Now, Calif, eat of thy treasure as much as thou wilt, since thou art so fond of it; for never shalt thou have aught else to eat!”
author: person:marco_polo
work: The Book of Ser Marco Polo, I.6, tr. Henry Yule (1903)
witness: Dictated in a Genoese prison around 1298, forty years after the event, by a Venetian who served the Mongols and never saw Baghdad's fall. The treasure-tower story is a moral fable (Persian sources say the caliph was trampled inside a carpet); it shows how the sack was told, not how it happened.

name: "Christians and spices": the Portuguese at Calicut
text: The first greeting that he received was in these words: “May the Devil take thee! What brought you hither?” They asked what he sought so far away from home, and he told them that we came in search of Christians and of spices. They said: “Why does not the King of Castile, the King of France, or the Signoria of Venice send hither?” He said that the King of Portugal would not consent to their doing so, and they said he did the right thing.
author: person:alvaro_velho
work: Roteiro of da Gama's first voyage, tr. E.G. Ravenstein (1898)
witness: The only eyewitness journal of the voyage, by an unnamed crew member. Its North African Moors who speak Castilian show how connected the ocean already was; the line about the King of Portugal is the Portuguese telling their own story.

sources.cite: A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497-1499 1898

name: The spice route from Calicut to Venice
text: From this country of Calecut, or Alta India,[196] come the spices which are consumed in the East and the West, in Portugal, as in all other countries of the world, as also precious stones of every description. The following spices are to be found in this city of Calecut, being its own produce: much ginger and pepper and cinnamon, although the last is not of so fine a quality as that brought from an island called Çillan [Ceylon],[197] which is eight days journey from Calecut. Calecut is the staple for all this cinnamon. ... The Mecca vessels carry these spices from there to a city in Mecca[199] called Judeâ [Jidda], and from the said island to Judeâ is a voyage of fifty days sailing before the wind, for the vessels of this country cannot tack. At Judeâ they discharge their cargoes, paying customs duties to the Grand Sultan.
author: person:alvaro_velho
work: Roteiro of da Gama's first voyage, tr. E.G. Ravenstein (1898)
witness: A Portuguese account of the route they meant to bypass, gathered from informants at Calicut in 1498. It describes the Mamluk Red Sea system accurately; its listing of every customs post served the case for the Cape route.

sources.cite: A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497-1499 1898

name: Barbosa on Malacca, the richest port in the world
text: Many Moorish merchants reside in it, and also Gentiles, particularly Chetis, who are natives of Cholmendel: and they are all very rich and have many large ships, which they call jungos. ... so that this city of Malaca is the richest trading port and possesses the most valuable merchandise, and most numerous shipping and extensive traffic, that is known in all the world.
author: person:duarte_barbosa
work: A Description of the Coasts of East Africa and Malabar, tr. H.E.J. Stanley (1866)
witness: Written around 1516 by a Portuguese clerk in Malabar, from a Spanish manuscript translated by Stanley in 1866 (the attribution to Barbosa is disputed). Its praise of Malacca justified the Portuguese conquest of 1511; the list of Gujarati, Tamil (Cheti), Chinese and Javanese traders is confirmed by Tome Pires.

name: Mouhot on Angkor Wat
text: One of these temples--a rival to that of Solomon, and erected by some ancient Michael Angelo--might take an honourable place beside our most beautiful buildings. It is grander than anything left to us by Greece or Rome, and presents a sad contrast to the state of barbarism in which the nation is now plunged. ... if you interrogate the Cambodians as to the founders of Ongcor-Wat, you invariably receive one of these four replies: “It is the work of Pra-Eun, the king of the angels;” “It is the work of the giants;” “It was built by the leprous king;” or else, “It made itself.”
author: person:henri_mouhot
work: Travels in the Central Parts of Indo-China (1864)
witness: A French naturalist's journal, published after his death in 1861 and edited for a European public. His contrast between ancient grandeur and present "barbarism" founded the colonial myth of a lost city and a degenerate people, which modern archaeology (Penny, Carter) refutes: Angkor Wat was never abandoned.
